decisions.reason: Keeps the sense that responsibility leaves no option to retreat in natural, direct language.
The Korean says he put the First Elder down; “let go” changes the physical action.
Keeps the wind vanishing in the nearby heat; dropping “the” does not change the image.
Names the spear shaft explicitly, as the Korean does, without changing the action.
Keeps the falling Force and simultaneous response while breaking up a crowded sentence.
Preserves time surging forward like a torrent after the crash in natural phrasing.
The Korean says the ground’s surface flipped over; “tore open” changes the physical image.
Keeps the immediate realization of the strength gap without implying that Force itself collided.
Preserves the escalation from expected strength to unexpectedly greater strength.
The Korean calls the men in black far too powerful; “more than that” is vague and drops the judgment.
Keeps the same comparison and meaning with a natural change in clause order.
The breath is suppressed or muffled, not necessarily strained.
Preserves the Korean’s emphasis that this was only a momentary standoff.
“Just as it was now” preserves the comparison; “And then it did” adds a specific breaking point.
The Korean says the weapons met White Flame’s blade; “struck the spearhead” changes the contact.
Keeps the point that inherited energy and insight were not the only reasons he won.
Keeps the wolf-pack comparison; the past-tense narration is consistent with the surrounding prose.
The pack-based infamy is retained in the following hunk’s recast, so this redundant standalone line can go.
Retains the Qilian Three Fiends example and the pack-based source sense in a single natural sentence.
Restores “even now,” which the Korean uses to stress that they are closing in at this moment.
Restores the established “Three Elders of Tianshan” rendering and the location name.
Keeps the lost souls, increased strength, and obedience to one man in concise prose.
Preserves the approaching army’s roar and the Demon Lord’s clearly audible voice.
Keeps the speaker’s regret about Senior Jeok and his matter-of-fact contrast with the valuable prize.
The Korean says he could picture the face only faintly; “well enough” changes that degree.
Keeps the Demon Lord’s excitement about the coming sea of corpses and blood.
“Surrender quietly” naturally conveys the Korean request to surrender without resistance.
The Korean describes forcing his voice out, not specifically forcing out an answer.
Restores the explicit simultaneity of all three weapons flying into the air.
Keeps the four jiazi, superhuman body, soul-cost enhancement, and momentary reprieve.
Preserves the brief, likely unrepeatable opening in direct prose.
“Cut through them” fits the reveal that he actually cut the ghost horses in half.
Keeps the horses’ status as powerful monsters without the redundant intensifier.
Restores the source’s description of the sight as unbelievable.
Keeps the wish to explain and the immediate reason he cannot.
Preserves the mounts disappearing, the resulting opening, and the charge at the four enemies.
“Struck” naturally conveys the Korean’s forceful final attack.
Keeps the three attacks being blocked and Jeok Cheongang’s waiting palm strike.
Preserves the attack’s silence and its impact on a Black Ghost.
The Korean specifies that the blow hit the man in the chest; SOL drops that detail.
Keeps the brief correction to the attempted grin without changing its timing.
Preserves the expectation of death and the startling recovery in clear action prose.
Restores the lingering force of the Flame Divine Palm, rather than replacing it with a vague lasting mark.
Keeps the parry and spoken response without changing the action.
The Korean names Jeok Cheongang; retaining his name avoids dropping explicit identification.
Correctly identifies Jeok Cheongang as the one who knocked the earlier attacker away.
Keeps the Taishan comparison and its crushing-pressure image.
The Korean reports a fierce sound of air; “something cut through the air” adds an implied actor or object.
Keeps the saber knocking away the knives and the narrator’s rueful guess about Sama Pyo.
Preserves that Sama Pyo distracted only one enemy and still bought them breathing room.
Keeps the blast’s earth-shaking reach and its momentary concealment of the streak of light.
Preserves the knife’s flight from Sama Pyo’s hand, its landing in the throat, and its trembling.
The knife is already the clear referent of “it,” so the shorter line keeps the same sense.
The following dialogue supplies the speech; the recast keeps the knife removal and escape opening.
Keeps the earlier question and the Death Knight topic in natural dialogue.
The Korean’s blunt “bastards like that” carries profanity and attitude that SOL drops.
Keeps Sama Pyo’s calm arrival beside them without changing the action.
The source is a blunt exclamation, “What monsters,” not the flatter statement “They’re monsters.”
Restores “a bit,” preserving the Korean degree rather than making the comparison absolute.
Keeps the contrast that Maoshan-made jiangshi would count as native to this world.
Preserves both names for the Death Knights and the invasive-species image.
The period preserves the abrupt correction from future threat to damage already done.
Keeps the quiet groan being swallowed in concise, natural prose.
Keeps the point that the possibility no longer matters.
“Wreckage” is a natural recast of the rubble left by the collapsed rules.
Keeps the contrast between a few people and everyone included in “all of us.”
Preserves the approaching shouts reaching the group beside Jeok Cheongang and Sama Pyo.
The Korean presents the Wind-and-Cloud Sword Lord as approaching while invoking; SOL drops the approach.
Keeps the two swordsmen’s shared training under one master and the Zhongnan disciples.
Adds only a natural subject to the source’s introduction of another hard-faced man.
Keeps Sima Gong’s Gansu forces comparable in number and his somber gaze.
Preserves the pointed correction that Sima Gong was looking at Sama Pyo.
The following hunk restores the lips-parting and silence, so deleting this separate line loses no event.
Combines the silent hesitation with the final focus on the rulers from beyond the desert.
Keeps the Black Ghosts stopping together and the Demon Lord stepping forward with his army behind him.
The Korean says they should come out and face him; “come at me” changes this to an attack.
SOL changes the comparison from the Demon Lord’s bloodshed among the war’s worst to bloodshed rivaling fiends.
Keeps the blade’s Force joining together; the omitted people-in-the-way detail is carried by the next hunk.
Preserves that retreat is no longer possible and they must press ahead with all their strength.
The changed capitalization keeps the shouted cry without altering its force.
Keeps the emotions mingling and swelling in compact, readable prose.
Preserves the slow step amid the emotional turmoil with a natural recast.
“My heart beat” preserves the source’s simple beat without adding emphasis.
Keeps his pace quickening in response to the heart’s harsh, rapid rhythm.
The Korean says he summoned the raging gale; “a gale of my own” implies a separate gale.
Restores the source’s emphasis that the armies finally collided at the center.
Keeps the blood mist billowing and spreading as the superhumans push through the screams and deaths.
